case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old woman was seen in the cardiology clinic 1 month after being diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection during an emergency department visit for 2 days of shortness of breath and low-grade fevers. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram performed in the emergency department revealed no pulmonary infiltrates, effusion, or embolism but identified an isolated 4.2-cm dilatation in the mid ascending aorta (Figure 1). In the cardiology clinic, her blood pressure was 118/85 mm/Hg and heart rate 65/min. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated normal left and right ventricular function, a 4.3-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, and a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) without evidence of aortic stenosis or regurgitation (Figure 1). Family history revealed that her father had a dissection of the ascending aorta repaired at age 60 years.

options.B: Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast
options.C: Perform annual surveillance thoracic CT scans

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

dialogue_history.text: I disagree that urgent surgical repair is the most appropriate next step here. Current guidelines for ascending aortic aneurysms in a bicuspid aortic valve recommend surgical intervention at a diameter of ≥5.5 cm, or ≥5.0 cm with risk factors like family history or rapid growth. At 4.3 cm, this patient's aneurysm is below the threshold for prophylactic surgery. The next step should be medical management with beta-blockers and regular imaging surveillance.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.
